gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the yearly electricity cost of leaving each candidate on 24/7 as the house DNS and VPN box, worked out from each maker's rated idle draw at the 2026 US average residential rate (EIA, 18.19 ¢/kWh year to date). The range runs from about $5 a year for a Raspberry Pi 5 to $10 for a Synology DS225+ with its disks asleep, $20 for an Asustor AS5402T and $29 for a QNAP TS-264 with its drives in standby.
standout_why: Pages compared: racksandwatts.com's homelab guide and its DXP2800 vs DS225+ comparison, which give no wattage, running cost or price and don't mention Pi-hole, AdGuard or WireGuard; and starryhope.com's budget NAS guide, which gives one running cost (DXP2800 'about $10 a year' at 17 ¢ from OCinside's 7 W) and none for Synology, QNAP, Asustor, TerraMaster or a Pi. Our own current page lists idle power as 'not read' for the DS225+, TS-264, AS5402T, F2-425 Plus and Flint 2.
decides: Running 24/7 is the whole job here, so yearly power cost is the real gap between candidates. With disks asleep, the DS225+ (6.08 W, about $9.69 a year) and DXP2800 (about 7 W, about $11 a year) cost about the same to run. The QNAP TS-264 (18.288 W in disk standby, about $29 a year; 29.086 W operating, about $46) costs roughly 3× as much. Over 5 years that is about $146 to $232 for the QNAP against about $48 for the DS225+, which cancels a large part of the QNAP's main advantage, its native WireGuard server. A Pi 5 at about 3 W costs about $5 a year. That supports ChatGPT's advice to use a separate small box if the shopper doesn't need storage. One caution that is my own inference, not something a source said: the DS225+ has no NVMe storage pool (racksandwatts spec list), so Pi-hole or AdGuard containers would sit on the hard drives. Constant query logging could then stop the disks from sleeping, which moves it toward its 16.98 W access figure (about $27 a year). The DXP2800 can keep containers on NVMe.
